Nebraska law sets out when a person occupying land can claim title by adverse possession, and how an owner can remove someone who has no right to be there.

What the official sources say

  • An action to recover title or possession of land must be brought within ten years after the cause of action accrues. (Neb. Rev. Stat. 25-202(1); source)
  • A claimant of adverse possession must prove by a preponderance of the evidence actual, continuous, exclusive, notorious, and adverse possession under a claim of ownership for the full 10-year period (annotation to 25-202). (Neb. Rev. Stat. 25-202, annotations; source)

Nebraska Squatters Rights and Adverse Possession FAQ

Can a squatter take ownership of my Nebraska house?

Check the statute and talk to a Nebraska attorney about your facts.

How long does someone have to occupy Nebraska land before claiming it?

Ten years is the Nebraska number, and the clock only helps an occupant who meets every element of adverse possession for that entire period. The period comes from Neb. Rev. Stat. 25-202, which sets a ten-year limit for actions to recover title or possession of land.

The Nebraska Supreme Court has described what an occupant must show in a long line of cases collected under that statute. In Rentschler v. Walnofer (1979) the court required proof of actual, continuous, exclusive and notorious possession, adverse to the record owner and under a claim of ownership, for the full ten years. It also said the claimant must hold the land for a purpose to which it is adapted. The claimant carries the burden and must meet it by a preponderance of the evidence.

The sections reviewed here set no shorter period for squatters, and nothing in them gives a person title for simply moving into a vacant house for a few weeks. What a short-term intruder can do is create a possession problem the owner has to resolve through the courts or the police.

Government land follows different rules. Section 25-202(1) says no limitation applies to actions by a county, city, town, village, school or other listed public body to recover roads, streets, alleys, public grounds and town lots.

What kinds of occupation do not count as adverse possession?

Several common situations fail the test because the occupier never held the property against the owner's rights. Nebraska decisions listed in the annotations to 25-202 draw these lines.

SituationHow the cited case treats it
Living there with the owner's permissionPermissive possession cannot ripen into adverse possession until the change of position is brought home to the owner (Imperial Service Corp. v. Phipps, 1980)
A tenant who stays after the leaseA tenant cannot hold adversely until surrendering possession or giving the landlord unequivocal notice that the lease no longer governs (Kennedy v. Gottschalk, 1941)
A parent and child sharing a propertyPossession between parties in a parental or filial relationship is deemed permissive (Chase v. Lavelle, 1921)
A co-owner in possessionNotice of a claim to the entire estate must be brought home to the other co-owners plainly and unequivocally (Gramann v. Beatty, 1938)
A claim like a life estateThat is not a claim of ownership (Lewis v. Poduska, 1992)
An occupant who disclaims title earlyDisclaiming before the period runs bars an adverse possession claim (Weisel v. Hobbs, 1940)

These rules explain why a house that a relative or former renter has lingered in for years is not automatically lost. It also explains why owners are advised to put permission in writing and to react when a stay turns hostile.

Can a fence or a boundary mistake create a Nebraska adverse possession claim?

Yes, and boundary disputes are where adverse possession is most likely to matter for an ordinary homeowner. The annotations list several decisions on fences.

  • In Ohme v. Thomas (1938), parties who treated a fence as the boundary for the full ten years, without interruption, gained title to land that had been wrongly enclosed.
  • In Conkey v. Anderson Farms (1980), the court applied the same reasoning where a fence was built as a boundary line even though it was not the true one.
  • In Weiss v. Meyer (1981), the court said adverse possession rests on the occupant's intent as shown by acts, and that the intent can be mistaken. A claimant who occupies up to the wrong line believing it is the true line can satisfy the test.

For a seller, the lesson is practical. If a neighbor's garage, driveway or fence has sat over the line for a decade, that can surface in a survey or title review right when you are trying to close. A boundary fix, or a recorded agreement, is far easier to complete before an offer than during one.

How does an owner remove someone with no right to be in a Nebraska house?

The civil route is a forcible entry and detainer action, which starts with a written notice to leave. 25-21,220 lists who can be sued this way, including tenants holding over and, in subsection (5), a settler or occupier of land without color of title when the complainant has the right of possession.

Before filing, 25-21,221 requires the owner to notify the adverse party to leave. The notice must be served at least three days before the action begins, by leaving a written copy with that person or at the usual place of abode. If the person cannot be found in the county, the notice may be left at or posted on the premises. A Nebraska Court of Appeals decision, I. P. Homeowners v. Morrow (2003), calls that three-day notice necessary to obtain an order of restitution.

This remedy has limits. The Nebraska Supreme Court held in Woodsonia Hwy 281 v. American Multi-Cinema (2025) that a forcible entry and detainer case must be dismissed when the right to possession depends on resolving the defendant's own right in the property. A genuine title dispute belongs in a different action, such as one to quiet title, which is also subject to the ten-year statute under Olsen v. Olsen (2003).

When does an unwanted occupant become a criminal trespasser in Nebraska?

Entering or secretly remaining in a building knowing you have no license or privilege to do so is first degree criminal trespass, a Class I misdemeanor under 28-520. Second degree criminal trespass covers other places where notice against trespass has been given.

Under 28-521, notice can be given in three ways: by actual communication to the person, by posting in a manner prescribed by law or likely to come to the intruder's attention, or by fencing or enclosure designed to exclude intruders. Second degree trespass is a Class III misdemeanor, and it rises to a Class II misdemeanor if the person defies an order to leave that the owner or an authorized person communicates personally.

A person who walked in uninvited is in a different position from a former tenant or family member who once had permission. If the person once had permission, a written notice to leave and a copy of your deed give you a record of the order the statute refers to.

How can a Nebraska owner protect a vacant house?

The goal is to keep the ten-year clock from ever starting and to leave a paper trail if someone tests it. The statutes and cases above point to a few habits.

  • Inspect the property on a regular schedule and note dates, because the occupation must be actual, notorious and continuous to count against you.
  • Put any permission to stay in writing, including who may live there and until when.
  • Post notices and keep fences and locks in repair, which lines up with the notice methods in 28-521.
  • Serve the three-day written notice early if someone is staying without consent.
  • Record your own deed. The case Hadley v. Platte Valley Cattle Co. (1943) held that a fee simple holder under an unrecorded deed does not forfeit title by failing to assert it, but a recorded deed is easier for everyone to see.
  • Do not wait years. The annotations say death of the party against whom the statute is running does not stop it, so it continues against heirs (McNeill v. Schumaker, 1913).

That last point matters for inherited houses that sit empty while family members decide what to do.

Selling a Nebraska house with an occupant or a possession dispute

An occupied house is harder to sell on the open market, because a buyer is charged with notice of the rights of anyone in actual possession. That principle appears in the annotations to 76-238, which cite Grand Island Hotel Corp. v. Second Island Development Co. (1974) for the rule that a purchaser is charged with notice of a tenant's rights when the tenant is in actual possession.

For sellers, that means unresolved occupants and boundary claims tend to come up in a buyer's title review. We buy Nebraska houses as-is, including some with tenants, holdovers or messy ownership history, and we can talk through what a sale would look like. We are not lawyers, so if someone claims ownership of your property, speak with a Nebraska attorney first.

More questions about Nebraska Squatters Rights and Adverse Possession

Do squatters have rights in Nebraska?

Only if they satisfy adverse possession for ten full years under 25-202 and the cases interpreting it. The occupant must show actual, continuous, exclusive, notorious and hostile possession under a claim of ownership. An occupant who entered with the owner's permission generally cannot count that time.

How long is the adverse possession period in Nebraska?

Ten years. Section 25-202 limits actions to recover title or possession of land to ten years after the cause of action accrues, and Nebraska courts apply the same ten-year period to adverse possession claims.

What notice do I give a squatter in Nebraska before filing for eviction?

A written notice to leave, served at least three days before the action begins under 25-21,221. It may be handed to the person, left at the usual place of abode, or posted at the premises if the person cannot be found in the county.

Is it a crime to stay in someone's house in Nebraska without permission?

It can be. Entering or secretly remaining in a building knowing you are not licensed to do so is first degree criminal trespass under 28-520, a Class I misdemeanor. Defying a personal order to leave other property raises second degree trespass to a Class II misdemeanor under 28-521.

Can a former tenant claim my Nebraska house by staying after the lease ends?

Not by simply staying. Under the Kennedy v. Gottschalk decision cited with 25-202, a tenant cannot hold adversely to the landlord until surrendering possession or giving unequivocal notice that the lease no longer governs. Holdover tenants can also be removed through forcible entry and detainer under 25-21,220.

Last updated November 14, 2026.

Nebraska statutes set the basic rules between landlords and tenants, including deposits, notices and what happens when a rental is sold.

What the official sources say

  • Security deposit may not exceed one month's periodic rent, plus a pet deposit of up to one-fourth of one month's rent. (Neb. Rev. Stat. 76-1416(1); source)
  • The balance of the deposit and a written itemization must be delivered or mailed within fourteen days after termination of the tenancy. (Neb. Rev. Stat. 76-1416; source)
  • Month-to-month tenancy may be terminated by either party with written notice at least thirty days before the periodic rental date; week-to-week requires seven days. (Neb. Rev. Stat. 76-1437; source)
  • Landlord may enter without consent in an emergency; otherwise must give at least twenty-four hours' written notice and enter only at reasonable times. (Neb. Rev. Stat. 76-1423; source)
  • Landlord must comply with minimum housing codes affecting health and safety, make repairs after written or actual notice to keep the premises fit and habitable, and maintain plumbing, heating and electrical facilities. (Neb. Rev. Stat. 76-1419(1); source)
Selling in Nebraska?
We buy Nebraska houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

Which Nebraska law governs landlords and tenants?

Residential rentals in Nebraska fall under the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, which sits in Chapter 76 of the Nebraska Revised Statutes starting at section 76-1401. The act covers the whole life of a tenancy: the rental agreement, deposits, repairs, entry, termination, and the court case to recover possession.

The sections that come up most often for an owner who is thinking of selling are in the table below. The section titles are the Legislature's own.

SectionSubject
76-1416Security deposits and prepaid rent
76-1417Disclosure of the manager and the owner or owner's agent
76-1419Landlord to maintain fit premises
76-1425Noncompliance by landlord
76-1431Tenant noncompliance and failure to pay rent
76-1434Landlord liens and distraint prohibited
76-1439Retaliatory conduct prohibited
76-1440 to 76-1447Action for possession, from complaint to appeal

Owners who rent a house often ask whether the act changes when the property is for sale. The sections reviewed for this page do not say that listing a house ends a lease, so questions about a sale should be checked against the lease itself and an attorney.

What happens to the tenant's security deposit when a rental is sold?

The person who holds the landlord's interest when the tenancy ends is bound by the deposit rules. Section 76-1416(5) says so directly. A seller should therefore settle the deposit position with the buyer at closing, in writing, so that the new owner knows exactly what is being held.

The deposit rules themselves are specific.

  • The landlord applies prepaid rent and security to unpaid rent and to damages caused by the tenant's breach, then returns any balance with a written itemization within fourteen days after the tenancy ends.
  • If the tenant gave no forwarding address, the landlord mails the balance and itemization to the last-known address by first-class mail.
  • Money that comes back undeliverable, or stays unclaimed for one year, is treated as abandoned property reported to the State Treasurer.
  • A landlord who misses the deadline can owe the tenant the money plus court costs and reasonable attorney's fees. If the failure is willful and not in good faith, the tenant can also recover liquidated damages equal to one month's rent or twice the deposit, whichever is less.

A cash buyer who takes over a rental with tenants in place will usually ask for the lease, the deposit amount and the payment ledger. Having those documents ready speeds the closing.

What does a landlord have to tell the tenant about who owns and manages the home?

Section 76-1417 requires the landlord, or whoever signs the rental agreement for the landlord, to give the tenant in writing, at or before the start of the tenancy, the name and address of two people. One is the person authorized to manage the premises. The other is an owner, or a person authorized to act for the owner, for service of process and for receiving notices and demands.

When a rental changes hands, the tenant's notices may suddenly go to the wrong place. The statute speaks about the start of a tenancy and does not describe a handover, but it is sensible for a seller and buyer to give the tenant the new contact details in writing. That keeps rent, repair requests and notices from getting lost.

How can a landlord end a tenancy for nonpayment or a lease breach?

Nebraska uses a short notice for unpaid rent and a longer one for other breaches. Section 76-1431 sets out both. If rent is unpaid when due and the tenant does not pay within seven calendar days after written notice of nonpayment and of the landlord's intent to terminate, the landlord may terminate the rental agreement.

For a material breach of the rental agreement, or a breach that affects health and safety, the landlord delivers a written notice that names the acts or omissions. The notice says the agreement will end on a date not less than thirty days after receipt unless the tenant fixes the problem within fourteen days. If substantially the same breach comes back within six months, the landlord may end the agreement on at least fourteen days' written notice.

SituationWritten notice period
Rent unpaidSeven calendar days to pay
Material breach, first timeFourteen days to remedy; termination no sooner than thirty days after receipt
Same breach repeats within six monthsAt least fourteen days

These notices are a step before court. The Judicial Branch's landlord page adds that notice must be given to the adverse party three days before a forcible entry and detainer action is commenced, citing section 25-21,221. The act also gives tenants remedies for unlawful ouster and exclusion in section 76-1430, so shortcuts around the court process carry risk.

What can a tenant do if the landlord fails to keep the home livable?

The tenant has a mirror-image remedy in section 76-1425. For a material noncompliance by the landlord, or a failure to meet the repair duty in section 76-1419 that materially affects health and safety, the tenant may give written notice listing the problem. If it is not fixed within fourteen days, the rental agreement ends on a date not less than thirty days after the landlord receives the notice. A repeat of the same problem within six months allows termination on at least fourteen days' notice.

This matters to a seller because deferred repairs on a rental can produce a tenant who has a legal claim against the owner at the same moment a buyer is doing an inspection. A written repair history helps both sides. The act also has separate sections on failure to supply heat, water and essential services (76-1427), fire or casualty damage (76-1429), and the tenant's remedies for unlawful ouster or diminished service (76-1430).

Can a landlord retaliate or seize a tenant's belongings?

No on both counts, with limits. Section 76-1439 says a landlord may not retaliate by raising rent, cutting services, or bringing or threatening an action for possession after the tenant has complained to a government agency that enforces housing or building codes about a violation affecting health and safety, or after the tenant has joined or organized a tenants' union. A tenant who is retaliated against has the remedies in section 76-1430 and a defense to an eviction case. The statute still allows reasonable rent increases and changes in services.

Section 76-1434 adds that a landlord's lien or security interest in a tenant's household goods is not enforceable, and that distraint for rent is abolished. An owner preparing a rental for sale should never hold a tenant's property as leverage for unpaid rent.

The act also contains special rules for tenants who are victims of domestic violence, including release from the rental agreement and lock changes (sections 76-1431.01 to 76-1431.04). Those sections stand apart from any sale.

How does a court eviction work, and who can bring it?

The act has its own court procedure for recovering possession, running from the action for possession in section 76-1440 through the complaint, summons, trial and writ of restitution, to appeal in section 76-1447. Forcible entry and detainer cases are described by the Judicial Branch as proceedings for restoring possession of land to a person who has been wrongfully deprived of it.

One detail catches owners who hold rentals in a company. The Judicial Branch says that, except in Small Claims Court, a landlord that is a corporation or LLC cannot represent itself in court and must be represented by an attorney. The page also notes that court forms are not currently available for this category.

If a case is open, talk to the attorney handling it before signing a purchase agreement, and make sure the contract says whether the buyer takes the property occupied.

What should a Nebraska landlord do before selling a tenant-occupied house?

Selling a rental with a tenant inside is possible, and it is easier when the paperwork is in order. A few steps help most owners.

  • Pull the signed lease, any addenda, and the rent ledger.
  • Confirm the deposit amount, any pet deposit, and where the money is held.
  • Check that no notice of nonpayment or breach is half-finished, because the seven-day and thirty-day clocks run from written notice.
  • List open repair requests and complaints to a code office, since retaliation rules apply.
  • Give the tenant written contact details for the new owner and manager at closing.

If the tenant is behind or the home needs work, a buyer who purchases as-is can take the property in its current condition.

More questions about Nebraska Landlord Tenant Law and Tenant Rights

How much can a Nebraska landlord charge for a pet deposit?

Section 76-1416 allows a pet deposit of up to one-fourth of one month's periodic rent, on top of a security deposit that cannot exceed one month's rent. The cap does not apply to housing agencies under the Nebraska Housing Agency Act.

How long does a landlord have to give notice for unpaid rent?

Seven calendar days after written notice of nonpayment and of the intent to terminate. If the tenant does not pay within that time, the landlord may terminate under section 76-1431.

Who gets the deposit if the landlord sells?

The holder of the landlord's interest at the time the tenancy ends is bound by the deposit rules, so the new owner can be responsible. The seller and buyer should agree in writing at closing how the deposit is handled.

Can a tenant be evicted for complaining to the city about conditions?

Section 76-1439 prohibits retaliation, including bringing or threatening an action for possession, after a tenant complains to an agency that enforces housing codes about a health or safety violation. Reasonable rent increases are still allowed.

Can an LLC landlord file an eviction case without a lawyer?

According to the Nebraska Judicial Branch, a landlord that is a corporation or LLC cannot represent itself in court, except in Small Claims Court, and must be represented by an attorney.

content:
Nebraska Eviction Notice Rules: Notice Types, Days and Selling the House

Cash Offer in 24 Hours
  • Nebraska Eviction Notice Rules: inherited, behind on payments, tenants or repairs, we buy the house as-is
  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Nebraska Eviction Notice Rules sale
  • Turn the Nebraska Eviction Notice Rules offer down and you owe us nothing

Selling a Nebraska House? Get a Cash Offer

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Nebraska law requires a landlord to give a specific written notice before filing an eviction, and the number of days depends on the reason.

What the official sources say

  • Nonpayment: landlord may terminate if rent is unpaid and the tenant fails to pay within seven calendar days after written notice of nonpayment and intent to terminate. (Neb. Rev. Stat. 76-1431(2); source)
  • Lease violation: written notice that the agreement will terminate not less than thirty days after receipt if the breach is not remedied in fourteen days; if substantially the same breach recurs within six months, fourteen days' written notice. (Neb. Rev. Stat. 76-1431(1); source)
  • Violent criminal activity, illegal sale of controlled substances, or activity threatening others' health or safety allows suit for possession after five days' written notice with no right to cure. (Neb. Rev. Stat. 76-1431(4); source)
  • No-cause end of month-to-month tenancy requires written notice at least thirty days before the periodic rental date. (Neb. Rev. Stat. 76-1437(2); source)
Selling in Nebraska?
We buy Nebraska houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

How many days of notice does a Nebraska landlord have to give?

The number of days depends on the reason: 7 days for unpaid rent, 14 or 30 days for a lease violation, 5 days for serious safety problems, and 30 days to end a month-to-month tenancy. Each notice must be in writing.

ReasonWritten noticeCan the tenant fix it?Statute
Rent not paid7 calendar daysYes, by paying within the 7 days76-1431(2)
Material lease breachEnds not less than 30 days after receipt if not remedied in 14 daysYes, within 14 days76-1431(1)
Same breach again within 6 monthsAt least 14 daysNo cure period76-1431(1)
Violent crime, illegal drug sales, threats to safety5 daysNo right to cure76-1431(4)
Month-to-month, no cause30 days before the rental dateNot applicable76-1437(2)
Week-to-week, no cause7 days before the end dateNot applicable76-1437(1)

The notice only starts the process. A landlord who wants the tenant out still has to go to court.

What must a nonpayment notice say?

It must tell the tenant that rent is unpaid and that the landlord intends to end the rental agreement if the rent is not paid within seven calendar days. Both statements matter, because the statute ties the right to terminate to written notice of nonpayment and of that intention.

If the tenant pays in full inside the seven days, the landlord has no basis to terminate on that notice. Rent unpaid after the period lets the landlord end the agreement and move to the court step described below.

Nebraska's wording is a seven-day calendar count and not a business-day count, so weekends and holidays are included. Keep proof of how and when the notice was delivered, since the complaint later has to show compliance with the notice rules.

What is the difference between the 14-day and 30-day lease violation notice?

They are two parts of one notice. The landlord must give a written notice describing the acts or omissions that make up the breach, and the agreement ends on a date at least 30 days after the tenant receives it unless the tenant fixes the problem within 14 days.

The statute covers a noncompliance with the tenant's duties that materially affects health and safety, or a material breach of the rental agreement. If the breach can be remedied by repairs, paying damages or otherwise, and the tenant does so before the date in the notice, the agreement does not terminate.

  • A repeat of substantially the same problem within six months allows termination on at least 14 days' written notice, with no new chance to cure.
  • The landlord may also recover damages and seek an injunction for noncompliance.
  • If the tenant's noncompliance is willful, reasonable attorney's fees can be recovered.

When can a Nebraska landlord use the five-day notice?

The five-day notice applies when the tenant, a household member, a guest or anyone under the tenant's control engages in violent criminal activity, the illegal sale of a controlled substance, or other activity that threatens the health or safety of other tenants, the landlord or the landlord's employees. The tenant has no right to cure.

The statute lists examples that include physical assault or the threat of it, illegal use of a firearm or other weapon, possession of a controlled substance the tenant knew or should have known about, and conduct that threatens or causes property damage. The complaint must describe the incidents behind the suit.

There is a protection for tenants who are not the source of the problem. A landlord may not use this notice when the activity is by someone other than the tenant or a household member and the tenant takes steps such as seeking a protective order or reporting it to law enforcement. A perpetrator of domestic violence is not covered by that protection.

How does a month-to-month tenancy end without a reason?

Either side can end a month-to-month tenancy with written notice given at least 30 days before the periodic rental date named in the notice. A week-to-week tenancy needs at least seven days' written notice before the termination date.

If a lease has no fixed term, Nebraska treats the tenancy as month to month, or week to week for a roomer who pays weekly. That default can matter for a seller who inherited a house with someone living in it and no written lease.

A tenant who stays after the term or after termination without the landlord's consent can be sued for possession. If the holdover is willful and not in good faith, the landlord may also recover up to three months' periodic rent or threefold actual damages, whichever is greater, plus reasonable attorney's fees.

What happens in court after the notice period ends?

The landlord files a complaint for restitution with the clerk of the district or county court. The complaint must state the statutory authority for possession, the specific facts, a reasonably accurate description of the premises and the compliance with the notice rules.

  1. The court issues a summons with a copy of the complaint. It must be served within three days, not counting nonjudicial days, and is returnable within five days, not counting nonjudicial days.
  2. The case is tried by the judge without a jury.
  3. If judgment goes against the tenant, the court declares the rental agreement forfeited.
  4. At the landlord's request, the court issues a writ of restitution directing the constable or sheriff to restore possession on a date no more than ten days after the writ issues.

Only an officer under a writ returns possession. A notice alone does not change who has the right to be in the house.

What limits does Nebraska put on retaliation?

A landlord may not raise rent, cut services or bring or threaten an action for possession in response to a tenant complaining to a housing or building code agency about a violation that materially affects health and safety, or joining a tenants' union. A tenant who proves this has a defense to the possession case.

The same statute lists situations where the landlord can still sue. Those are when the code violation was caused mainly by the tenant's lack of reasonable care, when the tenant is behind on rent, or when compliance would need work that deprives the tenant of the unit. Reasonable rent increases remain allowed.

If a tenant dies, the landlord must make a reasonable attempt within ten days to reach the person the tenant named to retrieve belongings. That person then has 20 days after contact to say they will claim the property and 20 more days to remove it.

What does an eviction mean if you also want to sell the house?

An owner with a tenant has three paths: finish the notice and court process before listing, sell with the tenant in place, or sell to a buyer who takes the house as it stands. Which one fits depends on the lease, the stage of the case and how soon you need to close.

  • Keep copies of the lease, rent ledger, every notice and the proof of delivery.
  • Check whether the complaint, judgment or writ is still open, because those papers affect what a buyer is willing to take on.
  • For a deed recorded on or after July 18, 2026, plan for the $3.32 per $1,000 documentary stamp tax and a Form 521 filing.

This page summarizes Nebraska's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act notice rules and is not legal advice. Check the current statutes or speak with a Nebraska attorney before serving a notice.

More questions about Nebraska Eviction Notice Rules

How long is a Nebraska eviction notice for unpaid rent?

Seven calendar days. The landlord must give written notice of nonpayment and the intent to terminate, and the tenant can stop the termination by paying within that time.

Can a Nebraska landlord evict without going to court?

No. After the notice period the landlord must file a complaint for restitution, and only a constable or sheriff acting on a writ of restitution restores possession.

How long does a tenant have to leave after a judgment?

The writ of restitution must set a possession date no more than ten days after the writ is issued. The court issues it at the landlord's request after judgment.

What notice ends a month-to-month tenancy in Nebraska?

Written notice at least 30 days before the periodic rental date named in the notice. Either the landlord or the tenant can give it, with no reason required.

Does the tenant get a chance to fix a lease violation?

Yes, for most violations. The tenant has 14 days to remedy, and the agreement ends at least 30 days after receipt if the breach is not fixed. A repeat of the same breach within six months allows 14 days' notice without a cure period.

Is there a shorter notice for dangerous behavior?

Yes. Violent criminal activity, illegal sale of controlled substances or activity that threatens safety allows suit for possession after five days' written notice, with no right to cure.

Can a landlord retaliate if a tenant reports code violations?

Not by raising rent, reducing services or threatening a possession action over a health and safety code complaint, though the landlord can still sue for unpaid rent or other listed exceptions.
